DS Analysis: Allen's combination of downfield passing and rushing makes him a rare quarterback who can drive a dynasty lineup in more than one way. His grip on Buffalo's offense makes him a cornerstone for contenders and rebuilders alike.
Burrow's excellent 2026 passing has reinforced how much he can deliver without relying on his legs. As long as Cincinnati builds around him and Ja'Marr Chase, he's an elite dynasty quarterback.

Williams has become a more efficient passer in 2026, and young targets like Luther Burden III and Colston Loveland can grow alongside him. That gives Chicago's franchise quarterback a path to years of elite fantasy production.
Maye's downfield passing gives him a high ceiling even before you count what he adds as a runner. New England can build around both strengths, making him an elite long-term dynasty option.

Lawrence has taken a step forward as a passer under Liam Coen in 2026. The combination of better decision-making and useful mobility makes him a stronger multi-year investment than he was entering the season.

Mahomes has proven he can sustain a franchise offense even when the supporting cast changes. How often Kansas City can get him back to elite fantasy production matters more than the security of his long-term role.
Purdy's strong 2026 is another reason to trust his accuracy and timing as lasting strengths. He doesn't need to develop into a bigger rushing threat to stay a dynasty QB1 in San Francisco.

Daniels has protected the ball well in 2026 without giving up the rushing upside that makes him special. His ability to score in both phases keeps him in the dynasty elite, though durability remains a consideration.

Love has shown again in 2026 that Green Bay can lean on his arm for substantial production. His more modest rushing contribution limits his path to the very top of the position, but he has staying power as a dynasty starter.
Gibbs pairs game-breaking speed with the receiving volume to anchor a PPR roster for years. Detroit has him signed through 2030.
Goff's efficient 2026 has reinforced how well his accuracy fits Detroit's offense. He remains a strong target for teams trying to win without needing their quarterback to add rushing production.
Robinson doesn't need touchdowns to carry a fantasy lineup: his rushing and receiving roles both deliver. His Atlanta extension through 2030 gives that elite workload staying power.

Herbert's arm talent gives the Chargers a long-term answer at quarterback. For dynasty, there's a difference between trusting him to keep the job and assuming his offense will throw enough to make him an elite fantasy option.

Prescott's strong 2026 has shown what he can still deliver with established receivers in Dallas. He fits a contender that can use his passing production rather than a rebuild that needs a longer runway.
Chase can pile up catches underneath or score from anywhere, and Joe Burrow gives him the quarterback play to maximize both. He belongs at the top of any dynasty board regardless of roster window.

Nix's passing efficiency has lagged in 2026, even as Denver has invested in its receiving corps. His mobility keeps him useful in superflex, but his long-term ceiling depends on making more of the passing game.
Kansas City has given Walker the chance to make an impact as both a rusher and a receiver. Emmett Johnson can keep a share without knocking Walker out of the top dynasty tier.

Darnold's uneven 2026 is a reminder that his fantasy output can swing with his passing environment. Jaxon Smith-Njigba gives him a strong foundation in Seattle, but dynasty managers shouldn't assume an elite ceiling.

Injuries slowed Love's rookie year, but Arizona's draft investment and his three-down skill set give him one of the position's longest runways. He's a bet on the role he'll grow into, not the one he's played so far.

Smith-Njigba has turned an already strong target profile into elite production in 2026. He wins throughout the route tree, giving Seattle a receiver it can build around even when the offense leans on the run.
Stroud has been more efficient and less turnover-prone in 2026. That strengthens his multi-year outlook, although he still needs his arm to carry most of his fantasy value.

Injuries have disrupted Jackson's 2026, but his rushing can still change a fantasy matchup in a way few quarterbacks can match. He belongs in a multi-year dynasty core rather than being valued off this season alone.
Lamb has put together another strong season while sharing the field with George Pickens. Dallas doesn’t need to funnel every pass his way for Lamb to produce like a dynasty cornerstone.

Nabers has returned to a featured role in 2026, with the route running and burst to demand targets regardless of how the Giants’ offense evolves. He’s a receiver to build around, not simply a bet on Jaxson Dart.
Young has shown progress in 2026, and Tetairoa McMillan gives him a lead receiver who can develop with him. More consistent passing would move him beyond the superflex QB2 tier.
St. Brown still sets the pace for Detroit’s passing game. His chemistry with Jared Goff and ability to keep getting open underneath give him a PPR floor few receivers can match.

Jefferson’s scoring has suffered through Minnesota’s quarterback turnover, but he remains the receiver the offense looks to first. The underlying volume is a better gauge of his dynasty value than the recent fantasy results.
Cook's explosiveness and foothold in Buffalo's offense make him a strong multi-year starter. He's signed through 2029, though a smaller receiving role separates him from the elite dual threats.
London is producing yards in 2026 even though the touchdowns haven’t followed. His size and ability to draw targets make him a long-term WR1, with room for more if Atlanta improves its passing game.
Flowers has continued to draw targets through Baltimore’s quarterback changes. He can anchor a PPR lineup on catches and yardage, but steadier scoring would bring his ceiling closer to the top tier.
McBride’s steady volume gives him one of the safest PPR floors at any position. He’s the clear alternative to Bowers if you put a premium on dependable targets.

Bowers can win downfield or turn a short catch into a big play, giving him more ways to carry a fantasy lineup than most tight ends. He’s the top dynasty bet because he pairs that ceiling with years of runway.

Jeanty's receiving role has held up even when the rushing lanes haven't been there. If Las Vegas improves his surroundings, he has the skill set to move from a reliable PPR starter to a difference-maker.

Nacua’s ability to earn catches at every level gives him an unusually strong PPR floor for a receiver with his ceiling. The biggest long-term question is what the Rams’ passing game looks like after Matthew Stafford.
Taylor's extension keeps a proven workhorse in Indianapolis, where he can still anchor a contender. His career mileage makes the length of that window less certain than it is for the backs above him.

An injury-interrupted 2026 doesn't tell us much about how Mayfield's passing will age. He's a better fit for a contender that can use his established upside than for a rebuild paying for several more years of it.

Golden’s second-year breakout gives Green Bay another productive receiver alongside Christian Watson. He’s already showing he can win enough routes to hold his value without needing Watson out of the picture.
Mendoza's early NFL work is more useful for tracking his development than setting his ceiling. A young quarterback who can grow with Brock Bowers is worth patience, especially in superflex.

McMillan has established himself as Carolina’s lead receiver, using his size and body control to win even when the ball isn’t perfectly placed. More consistent quarterback play could push him into the top dynasty tier.

Loveland is growing into a reliable option for Caleb Williams without needing to be Chicago’s first read every week. The combination of youth and an expanding role gives him a shot at joining the elite tier.

Olave still earns volume and creates gains downfield, but Jordyn Tyson has given New Orleans a credible second option. Price Olave as a strong dynasty starter without assuming his old share of the passing game holds.

Collins still brings size, separation, and scoring upside to Houston’s passing game. Offensive inconsistency can make the ride bumpy, but he’s worth holding as a proven starter rather than selling off a down stretch.
Higgins has maintained strong production alongside Ja’Marr Chase rather than needing to replace him. The times he’s missed matter more to his dynasty floor than sharing Cincinnati’s targets.

Achane's receiving ability gives him an RB1 ceiling even without a workhorse carry share. Miami's commitment makes him worth waiting on after the ACL tear, but it's risky to price in a full return to form.
Warren can earn catches, but Indianapolis needs to use him farther downfield for those targets to produce a true difference-maker. His age and versatility give him time to get there.

Pickens gives Dallas a downfield threat who can also earn heavy volume when the matchup calls for it. He’s shown he can produce with Lamb, though his long-term value depends in part on where he plays beyond this season.
LaPorta can produce starter numbers without dominating Detroit’s targets. The Lions’ crowded offense makes his volume less predictable than the elite tier’s, but there’s plenty of runway left.
Fannin has already done enough as a receiver to build value independent of Cleveland’s quarterback play. His age and established role give him a higher ceiling than most of the veterans around him.
McCaffrey still separates from other win-now backs with what he can do as a receiver. Age and accumulated work make him a better fit for a title run than a rebuild.

Hall's Jets extension gives him stability, and his receiving ability can sustain strong PPR value in a split. Braelon Allen has shown enough that an uncontested workload isn't a safe long-term assumption.
Judkins has earned lead volume in Cleveland and shown enough as a receiver to avoid being boxed into an early-down role. Better rushing efficiency is what could move him into the next dynasty tier.
Likely has turned a lead receiving role with the Giants into difference-making fantasy weeks. If the volume becomes as steady as the upside is high, he can climb another tier.
Kraft’s ability to create yards after the catch gives him a way to produce without leading Green Bay in targets. A steadier volume floor would put him closer to the elite group.
Hampton leads the Chargers' rotation but hasn't turned that advantage into a clear workhorse role. His age and first-round investment give him time to separate and grow into a multi-year RB1.
Kincaid gets big gains on relatively modest volume, and playing with Josh Allen keeps the upside intact. Availability and a less dependable target share keep him below the top group.
Irving has reestablished himself as Tampa Bay's lead runner and can do damage without dominating every passing down. That makes him a strong multi-year starter even if the Bucs keep rotating in help.
Brown's passing-down role holds up better than his rushing efficiency, which keeps him valuable in PPR. His next contract is the swing factor in whether he retains a lead role beyond this season.
Tate has earned a meaningful role in Tennessee without needing the Titans to score often. The way he tracks the ball and wins outside makes him a good bet to grow with Cam Ward.

An injury-disrupted 2026 doesn't erase Hurts' ability to swing games as a runner, especially near the goal line. The value of that rushing role makes him worth holding, even if how it ages over several seasons is less certain.

Coleman's power and receiving ability give him a credible shot at becoming Denver's lead back of the future. His dynasty value hinges on locking down that job rather than settling into a rotation with RJ Harvey.

Williams' receiving role and extension through 2028 protect his value as the Rams split more carries with Blake Corum. He's still a useful multi-year starter without counting on another workhorse season.

Seattle's first-round investment gives Price a long runway to claim the backfield. He hasn't separated from Zach Charbonnet yet, so the upside is easier to see than the path to consistent weekly volume.
Watson’s downfield production gives him a high ceiling without needing the most catches in Green Bay. Golden adds target competition, but their emergence together shows both can have lasting value.

Washington has turned his opportunity into real yardage and scoring in Jacksonville. There’s plenty of competition for catches, but he’s shown too much to price as a player who only benefits when others sit.

Penix's downfield arm is worth holding in superflex, but his uneven 2026 hasn't settled the question of whether he can lead Atlanta for years. More consistent passing efficiency would do more for his dynasty value than another flash throw.

Tuten has turned an opening in Jacksonville into a meaningful lead role, and his speed can make limited space go a long way. Chris Rodriguez's short-yardage work is the main check on Tuten's scoring ceiling.

Tyson has shown how quickly his size and run-after-catch ability can translate into NFL targets. The sample is still small, but the receiving upside is worth buying even with Olave established in New Orleans.

Wilson keeps finding ways to earn targets in an uneven Jets passing game. Better quarterback play would raise the ceiling, but he already has a role that can carry your PPR lineup for several seasons.

Concepcion has earned useful work early in Cleveland, where his quick routes and ability after the catch help him create his own yards. His future looks brighter than the current quarterback situation suggests.
Lemon is already useful underneath, where his hands and ability to finish catches in traffic show up. More chances downfield would move him from a solid PPR asset toward a higher-end dynasty starter.
Hubbard has reclaimed the lead role in Carolina, with receiving work to support him when the team can't lean on the run. He's signed through 2028 and fits contenders better than long rebuilds.
Sadiq’s burst gives him a way to win against coverage even before he becomes a polished route runner. The Jets’ investment makes him worth holding while he works to separate from Mason Taylor.

Burden has capitalized on Chicago’s available targets, pairing short-area volume with the burst to score from distance. He’s a better long-term bet now that the production is catching up to the talent.

Shough has shown he can handle a meaningful passing workload in 2026. Chris Olave and Jordyn Tyson give him a foundation, but better efficiency would make him easier to trust as a multi-year superflex starter.

Rice has already shown what he can do with high-percentage targets from Patrick Mahomes. The Chiefs’ added competition makes that volume harder to project, so don’t pay as if an elite share is guaranteed.

Ward's ability to extend plays is worth developing, even in a difficult 2026. His long-term superflex case rests on turning that creativity into steadier passing production as he and Carnell Tate grow together.

Smith’s season has been uneven, and Makai Lemon has made the most of Philadelphia’s available work. Smith’s ability to separate at different depths still gives him a path back to lead-receiver production.
Williams still creates the kind of long gains that can swing a matchup. With St. Brown handling the steadier reception volume, treat Williams as a high-upside starter rather than a PPR floor play.

Dart showed early in 2026 how his arm and legs can put pressure on a defense before a knee injury interrupted his development. The dual-threat ceiling is worth betting on, but the limited NFL sample still leaves real risk.

Odunze is still producing downfield with Caleb Williams even as Burden gets more of the short-area work. His spike weeks have value, but growing into a consistent PPR starter will require steadier volume.
Boston has given Cleveland a productive outside receiver whose catch radius and vertical game complement Concepcion. He doesn’t need to win the slot targets to grow into a regular dynasty starter.

Egbuka hasn’t turned an open Tampa Bay depth chart into a steady featured role. He’s young enough to recover the value he showed early in his career, but his current price should leave room for that to take time.

Pitts can still threaten defenses downfield, and Atlanta’s commitment gives him time to make that production more consistent. At 26, there’s room for another step without paying for the ceiling up front.

Willis' rushing makes him more interesting than most quarterbacks still proving themselves as passers. Injuries have interrupted that evaluation in 2026, so price in the chance Miami never commits to him long term.
McConkey’s recent production hasn’t matched the ceiling he showed as a rookie. His route running still fits Justin Herbert, making him a good buy if the trade price no longer assumes a featured role.

Kittle can still make a contender better without needing to lead San Francisco in targets. He ranks behind the younger top options because you’re buying fewer future seasons, not because he’s lost the ceiling.
Waddle gives Denver a receiver who can win downfield and generate yards after the catch. He doesn’t have a clear lead role yet, but his separation gives him room to outlast the current depth chart.

Cooper’s hands and ability to run through contact give him a way to earn work without needing to be the Jets’ primary deep target. Wilson is still the lead receiver, so buy Cooper for what he can become rather than what he can deliver now.

Bernard can play inside or outside and has the hands to be a reliable target in either spot. Pittsburgh’s veteran receivers limit the immediate opportunity, but that versatility gives him a way to grow into their roles.

Moore gives Buffalo an experienced receiver who can create after the catch without relying on deep throws. His fit with Josh Allen is useful to contenders, with less upside for teams that need a longer runway.

Brown’s first season in New England has been quiet, leaving plenty of projection in the rebound case. Drake Maye helps that case, but Brown is a better buy for a contender that can get him at a discount.

Corum has been efficient enough with his share to offer more than handcuff value. How much he can chip away at Kyren Williams' role will determine whether he's a regular fantasy starter or a strong reserve.

Williams’ route running and hands have given him a way into Washington’s offense. He’s an affordable stash for the eventual opportunity behind its veteran receivers, not a player to buy for immediate volume.

Mayer has shown he can contribute as a receiver alongside Brock Bowers, and Las Vegas extended him. His upside depends on the Raiders sustaining two useful tight end roles rather than on Mayer moving to a new team.
Lane has shown he can turn his length and speed into meaningful downfield work for Baltimore. The next step is earning those targets often enough to start him with confidence.
Raridon’s blocking can earn him snaps while he develops as a receiver behind Hunter Henry. The payoff would be a regular role with Drake Maye, not just a place in New England’s rotation.

Stowers profiles as a slot-style receiver, which gives him a path to catches even if he never becomes a traditional every-down tight end. Dallas Goedert is still the immediate hurdle to steady volume.
Wilson has backed up his breakout by earning steady catches in Arizona. Harrison’s departure makes the target path clearer, even if Wilson doesn’t offer the same scoring ceiling as the top receivers.
Henry's goal-line value still plays for a contender even as his rushing efficiency slips. At this stage, price him for the points he can score now rather than for a long starting runway.

Jacobs still has the profile of a lead runner when available, but a disrupted season exposed how quickly his role can come into question. He's more attractive for a title run than a roster looking several years out.

Metcalf’s size and open-field strength still make him dangerous, but the Pittsburgh passing game hasn’t consistently turned that into a strong fantasy floor. He’s a better buy as veteran depth than as a bet on returning to elite volume.
Skattebo has shown he can handle meaningful carries after a serious ankle injury. A bigger passing-game role would make him less dependent on winning the Giants' early-down work every season.

Freiermuth is Pittsburgh’s more natural receiving option at tight end, but Darnell Washington’s presence keeps the work from consolidating. A larger route share would lift his value more than another streak of TDs.
Monangai has been effective enough to earn more carries on merit. D'Andre Swift's extension makes a takeover less straightforward, so Monangai's value depends on how big a share he can win.
Barkley still has the talent to swing a fantasy matchup, but injuries have narrowed the case for several more elite seasons. Treat him as a contender buy rather than a rebuild cornerstone.
Strange has settled into a productive role and has Jacksonville’s long-term backing. More scoring-area targets would give him a path from a useful starter to a higher-ceiling one.
Johnson has already shown he can win targets in New Orleans, but the Saints have younger options taking on more of the passing game. He’s a better fit for a contender’s bench than a rebuild.

Coker can earn catches underneath and create useful gains out of the slot when Carolina looks his way. The weekly volume is less secure than McMillan’s, making Coker better as a young depth piece than a core starter.

Hockenson can still earn enough targets to start when healthy. Durability and Minnesota’s unsettled quarterback situation make his future value less secure than his receiving talent alone would suggest.

Johnson has already shown he can contribute as a receiver and handle lead carries when needed. Kenneth Walker limits the immediate path, but Johnson can earn PPR value without waiting for the starting job.

Williams' Dallas deal and role near the goal line give contenders a dependable source of rushing volume. His dynasty case rests more on keeping those valuable touches than on producing explosive plays.

Addison can win downfield opposite Jefferson, which makes him useful without lead-receiver volume. He’s worth holding for that upside, though Minnesota’s uncertain passing game limits what you should pay today.
Andrews can still deliver when Baltimore leans on him. At 31, the bet is on useful starts for a contender, not a return to his peak dynasty value.
Schultz offers useful catch volume in Houston without much explosive upside. He’s a sensible short-term starter to have on hand rather than a player to build around.
Thomas’ rookie tape still makes a rebound believable, but Washington and Meyers have made Jacksonville less dependent on him. Buy at a price that leaves room for him to stay a complementary receiver.

Johnston can still generate long gains with Justin Herbert, but his catch volume has been light. His dynasty value depends on converting those shots into a wider role rather than living off splash plays.
Henry can still give a contender catches rather than relying entirely on touchdowns. His extension brings stability, but at his age the value is in lineup help, not resale upside.

McLaurin still gives Washington a vertical target who can produce with Jayden Daniels. The veteran-heavy receiver room and his career stage make him more valuable to a contender than a rebuilding team.
Brazzell’s size and long speed are worth a stash, but Carolina hasn’t had a chance to establish an NFL role for him. Keep the investment small until his routes give you something concrete to value.

Evans still gives San Francisco a way to score downfield and near the goal line. He can help a contender when available, but at this stage the trade price shouldn’t assume anything beyond short-term production.
Adams still gives the Rams an experienced scorer who can win before and after the catch. Buy him for the points he can help you score now, not for a role that depends on Stafford staying in place.
Okonkwo can create yards after the catch, but Washington has to give him enough routes for that skill to matter consistently. He’s a useful depth option without a reliable every-week floor.
Black has earned real work behind Christian McCaffrey and gives San Francisco a possible in-house successor. He's worth holding for that opening, not valuing as if he already has the job.
Kelce still has the chemistry with Patrick Mahomes to help a contender. At his age, the risk of losing the entire asset outweighs what you’d normally pay for that production.
Douglas has already shown his size can produce chunk gains in Miami. More consistent separation would help him turn that into a role you can trust between the big plays.
Goedert remains useful near the goal line, but the Eagles have a younger receiving option in Eli Stowers. Age and contract uncertainty make him a better win-now option than a long-term hold.
Ferguson has the athleticism to make plays when the Rams give him routes, but their rotation hasn’t made him a reliable receiving option. He’s a patient stash, not someone to count on for starts.

Swift's extension through 2029 gives Chicago every reason to keep him involved, with scoring and receiving work to fall back on. Kyle Monangai makes another stretch of dominant backfield volume less likely.
Flournoy has kept producing in a Dallas offense built around Lamb and Pickens. That gives him a better dynasty case than the typical injury fill-in, even if he’s not a weekly starter yet.
Barner has earned a role in Seattle without needing to out-test Elijah Arroyo. His fantasy ceiling depends on turning that playing time into a bigger share of the passing game.

Pearsall has the route skills to matter, but San Francisco’s veteran additions have made his path less certain. Treat him as a stash with room to regain value rather than assuming he still has a starter’s role.

Stafford can still make the most of a receiver like Puka Nacua, so his passing has value to a team chasing a title. The Rams' investment in Ty Simpson makes it harder to justify paying for several more years of starts.
Etienne's multi-year Saints deal and receiving skills give him a useful PPR floor. Until he separates from the rest of the backfield, he projects more as flexible depth than as a dynasty starter.
Dell’s separation and route craft keep a bounce-back case alive. Houston’s added depth means he has to earn his way back into regular routes before you count on the production.
Stribling’s hands and vertical ability give San Francisco something to develop behind its veterans. Hold him where you can wait for more routes, since speed alone won’t unlock steady usage.
Gadsden is young enough to win back a receiving role with Justin Herbert, but Charlie Kolar and David Njoku are real competition. He’s more interesting as a stash than as a player to start.
Helm has a path to becoming Tennessee’s best receiving tight end, but Daniel Bellinger makes the workload less predictable. Bet on the possibility of more routes, not a guaranteed starting job.
Bell’s strength through contact gives Miami a reason to keep developing him after an encouraging start. More regular routes are the key to turning that ability into fantasy value.
Pierce can produce a big week on a handful of deep chances, but his current volume leaves little room for error. He’s easier to roster in best ball than to rely on in a weekly lineup.
Allen proved he could hold up on lead volume while Breece Hall was out. Hall's extension makes that role harder to reach again in New York, but Allen is young enough to have time for another opening.
Warren has shown he can carry Pittsburgh's backfield and stay productive through the air. The long-term question is how much of that work he can keep alongside Rico Dowdle.
Bryant can win on intermediate routes, but Waddle’s arrival gives Denver little reason to rush him into a bigger job. He’s a patient depth buy if the price leaves room for more competition.
Dallas has committed to Ferguson, and Dak Prescott can still find him near the goal line. He needs more weekly targets to become a reliable PPR starter rather than a touchdown bet.
Otton’s extension and blocking make his snaps in Tampa Bay safer than his fantasy role. He’s useful depth, but his ceiling won’t change unless he earns more valuable targets.

Hunter’s receiving talent still gives him upside, but his limited production and possible defensive workload make a future full-time WR role hard to price. He’s a stash for teams that can afford to wait.

Charbonnet's short-yardage work gives him a way to score even as Seattle develops Jadarian Price. His next contract will matter more than his current depth-chart spot for projecting the next few seasons.

Sarratt’s college scoring showed he can finish catches in traffic, but his role in Baltimore hasn’t given him many chances yet. He’s worth holding in deep leagues for the opportunity to grow into an outside job.

Stevenson still gives New England productive touches as a runner and receiver. Age, knee trouble, and younger competition make it easier to buy his near-term role than to count on it for several more years.

Croskey-Merritt has the early-down ability to matter, but he hasn't distanced himself from the rest of Washington's backfield. Without a clearer lead role or more targets, he's a depth bet rather than a weekly starter.
Hurst has flashed the size and downfield ability that made him an interesting prospect. He’s best held in deep leagues while Tampa Bay sorts out who will earn the long-term outside work.
Pittman gives Pittsburgh a physical possession receiver alongside Metcalf. His value rests on the team giving him enough catches to offset modest downfield production.
Worthy can force defenses to cover more ground, but Kansas City has other receivers for the short, repeatable targets. His value rises if he can earn regular looks beyond the designed shots.

Ayomanor gives Tennessee size outside, where he can win downfield without overlapping much with Wan’Dale Robinson. Tate’s arrival makes it harder for Ayomanor to grow into a large share of the passing game.
Gordon has shown he can absorb lead carries in Miami. His dynasty ceiling depends on whether he keeps a meaningful rushing role when De'Von Achane is back.
Meyers gives Jacksonville a reliable receiver who can operate in several parts of the field. He makes more sense as veteran depth for a contender than as a player to acquire for future growth.
Mitchell’s size and speed make him an effective downfield complement to Wilson. More consistent targets, not just a few big plays, are what would make him dependable in PPR.
Klare’s route running gives him a chance to carve out an underneath role. There are enough tight ends competing for Rams snaps to make him a taxi-squad hold rather than a near-term starter.
Dike’s return ability helps him stay involved, but his receiving work hasn’t grown enough to change his fantasy outlook. Hold him where the bench can accommodate a bet on a bigger route role.

Mason can handle a run-heavy workload when Minnesota needs him, but his limited receiving role keeps the floor low. He's worth stashing for a backfield opening, not penciling in as the eventual starter.
Henderson hasn't overtaken Rhamondre Stevenson, and an illness interrupted his second season. His burst and receiving ability still give New England reasons to expand his role over time.

Harrison’s move to Houston gives him a fresh start but doesn’t resolve the separation or target-volume concerns. Buy the talent only at a price that accounts for Nico Collins and the rest of the receiver room.

Sutton still gives Bo Nix a big target in scoring situations, but Waddle’s arrival cuts into the long-term runway. He’s a better fit for teams buying veteran production than teams building their next core.
Dulcich has the receiving skills to make good use of downfield routes in Miami. An unsettled long-term role makes him a depth flier rather than a core dynasty piece.
Washington earned a meaningful rushing role even with Ashton Jeanty ahead of him. He's a useful stash because the Raiders have shown they'll play him without an injury opening the door.
Delp can get on the field as a blocker or by moving around the formation. His fantasy value depends on New Orleans turning that flexibility into routes, not just more snaps.

Higgins brings size and contested-catch ability, but Houston added more competition for the outside routes he needs. He’s worth holding at a development price, not one that assumes a future starting job.

Coleman still has the size and scoring upside to matter with Josh Allen. Buffalo’s deeper receiver room makes a volume breakout less certain, so hold him as a bet on growth rather than an established starter.

Fields’ size and ability to finish in traffic give the Giants a different outside option from Nabers. His dynasty case depends on turning that role into meaningful volume rather than just contested opportunities.
Branch’s quickness makes him useful on manufactured touches, but those plays haven’t added up to much receiving production. His dynasty value depends on becoming a regular route runner in Atlanta.
Johnson still has athletic upside, but Isaiah Likely has taken the valuable receiving work in New York. A new role would matter more for his dynasty value than another run of touchdowns.
Boerkircher’s blocking and draft investment give him a path to playing time. With Brenton Strange extended, he’ll have to earn meaningful routes rather than wait for a vacancy.
Shakir is a dependable underneath option for Josh Allen, but Buffalo’s deeper receiver room makes a volume jump harder to project. He’s worth having for PPR depth rather than chasing as a breakout.
Engram’s routes underneath can still help a real offense. Dynasty managers shouldn’t pay for the volume he once handled without evidence Denver will give him that kind of role.
Tucker has turned speed into meaningful production for Las Vegas. The yards come in chunks, which makes him useful in deeper leagues even if he never becomes a dependable high-catch starter.
Arroyo can stretch the field, but A.J. Barner has given Seattle a reason to keep the work split. Stash the athletic upside without counting on the team to hand over the job.
Downs wins early in routes and gives Kansas City another receiver who can get open underneath. He has long-term PPR utility, but Rice is a real obstacle to a large share of that work.

Harris has already given the Chargers useful production outside, where his size separates him from the other young wideouts. More scoring opportunities and regular routes could turn him into a starter without a huge change in role.
Gesicki can still turn limited routes into a useful spot start when Cincinnati’s offense is humming. His age and the competition for targets leave little reason to pay for more than that.

Dowdle has shown he can produce with a starter's workload, and his Pittsburgh deal gives him a place to contribute. With Jaylen Warren in the way, he's more valuable as injury insurance than as a succession bet.

Marks has earned carries in Houston, but David Montgomery makes it hard to count on feature volume. The lasting PPR upside is in claiming passing downs, not just getting a larger slice of early downs.

Godwin can still catch passes underneath, but the explosive gains and scoring that once added to that role have been harder to find. Buy the catches cheaply rather than banking on a return to his old peak.
Parkinson has useful scoring-area work in the Rams’ rotation, but the offense can spread targets across several tight ends. He’s a deeper-league option until that role becomes more consistent.

Bateman gives Baltimore another downfield option, but Flowers and Lane have shown they can draw more attention from the quarterback. He needs a bigger weekly role before a QB change can do much for his value.

Harvey's receiving flashes offer a path to PPR value even if Denver gives Jonah Coleman more of the rushing work. He needs to secure a clear passing-down role before he can be counted on in fantasy lineups.
Klein’s blocking can get him developmental snaps before he’s ready to earn targets. Houston’s incumbent options give him time to grow, but prevent a clear path to fantasy production.
Noel has made the most of his chances in Houston, where he can turn limited catches into chunk gains. More regular targets are the next test in a crowded receiver room.

Brooks' draft pedigree and receiving potential are still worth a stash after multiple injuries. With Chuba Hubbard established ahead of him, the first step is earning a steady role, not competing for the entire backfield.
Kolar’s blocking explains why the Chargers trust him with starter snaps. He needs those snaps to turn into regular routes and targets before they matter in fantasy.
Washington’s size and ability after the catch make him more interesting than a typical blocking tight end. His value rises if Pittsburgh uses him on more routes, not just in heavier packages.

Franklin’s downfield ability still gives him a role to chase, but his receiving work has faded with Waddle in Denver. That makes him a discounted hold rather than a young receiver to buy at breakout prices.
Horton has shown enough to compete for complementary work in Seattle. The path is earning routes opposite Smith-Njigba, not overtaking him, so keep expectations in line with that role.
Wilson has contributed when Pittsburgh puts him on the field, including in scoring situations. The veteran additions make a breakout less likely, but he’s worth tracking if more routes open up.
Taylor can be a reliable underneath target, but Kenyon Sadiq gives the Jets another young tight end to feature. He needs to retain more of the passing work to justify a shallow-league roster spot.
Thomas can create on designed touches, but Chicago has plenty of young receiving talent to develop. He’s a deep stash until he shows he can earn targets without the play being drawn up for him.
Shaheed’s speed is useful even on a small route share, but his catches haven’t been steady enough to trust each week. That profile is easier to use in best ball than in a traditional PPR lineup.
Brown’s speed gives New Orleans a reason to use him on returns and in space. Until it earns him a regular receiving role, the big-play ability is more useful to his NFL team than to a dynasty lineup.
Pollard can still supply reliable carries for a contender, but he'll need a new deal after 2026. It's hard to project similar volume elsewhere as he moves into the later part of his career.
Doubs has given New England downfield production without a large catch total. His fit with Maye is worth holding onto, but consistent work is more important to his future than the early scoring.
Njoku’s receiving ability keeps him relevant when the Chargers need it. Age and competition in that tight end room make him a short-term reserve rather than a long-term upside play.

Lance offers size and vertical ability, but Olave and Tyson leave little immediate room for steady outside work in New Orleans. Hold him in deeper leagues if you can wait for that opportunity to develop.
Diggs has shown he can still turn his opportunities into scores in Washington. His value is in the points he can deliver to a contender now, not what he might be worth in several seasons.

Samuel can still create explosive plays in the passing game or on designed runs. San Francisco can put that to use without giving him a lot of targets, which makes him a better win-now option than a long-term hold.
Roush’s blocking gives him a useful role alongside Colston Loveland. It may earn real playing time without giving him the receiving work a dynasty stash needs.

Simpson is a bet on eventually getting a chance to succeed Matthew Stafford, not a guarantee that he inherits the Rams' job. He makes sense on a patient superflex roster that can wait to see how he develops.
Higbee can still earn catches as part of the Rams’ rotation. With his age and younger options in the room, his value is mostly as a fill-in.
Waller can still give a contender receiving production that’s hard to find at the bottom of the position. There’s little reason to value him for more than the short window in which he can help.

Reed can still create yards after the catch, but Watson and Golden have earned major roles while his own work has dwindled. Bet on the talent only at a price that reflects the routes he still needs to win back.
TeSlaa’s size and ability to make long catches give Detroit a different option behind its main receivers. He has upside if that role grows, but limited catches make him hard to start regularly.
Koziol showed enough as a college receiver to justify a deep stash. Brenton Strange’s extension and Nate Boerkircher’s presence leave him several steps from regular work.

Washington has earned steady underneath work in Miami, which gives him more of a PPR floor than the downfield specialists around him. A bigger scoring role would change the case for making him a regular start.
Rodriguez can hold a role as Jacksonville's short-yardage complement to Bhayshul Tuten. The touchdown opportunities make him useful depth, but little receiving work limits his long-term ceiling.
Cameron has made a scoring impact on limited work, putting his college ball skills to use. The next step is earning enough routes to make that production repeatable in Jacksonville.
Sanders has time to develop, but Carolina has spread its tight end usage elsewhere. A meaningful increase in routes would be a better buying signal than a one-game line.

Douglas has been New England’s most productive receiver in 2026, using speed from the slot to do more than just collect short catches. That gives him a case for staying useful as the veterans return to the rotation.
Wicks has translated his separation into downfield gains in Philadelphia. The long-term upside is there if he can keep earning routes with Smith and Lemon in the mix.

Vele has shown he can handle an everyday receiving role, but Tyson’s emergence threatens the targets that made it valuable. Hold him as a depth option without counting on the same workload going forward.
Gainwell's receiving versatility gives him a chance to retain PPR utility as rosters change. In Tampa Bay, Bucky Irving keeps his upside closer to useful depth than a starting job.
Spears' receiving skill can keep him relevant in PPR even with Tony Pollard ahead of him on the ground. The next contract is an opportunity to improve his role, not a reason to assume a breakout.
Boutte has turned limited work into useful downfield production for Houston. He needs a larger share of the routes to turn that efficiency into dependable dynasty value.
Kmet can help Chicago in two-tight-end sets without challenging Colston Loveland for targets. His clearest path back to fantasy relevance is a change in role or team.
Fant has the movement skills to handle more receiving work if New Orleans needs him. Until he earns a meaningful share alongside Juwan Johnson, he belongs on deep rosters only.
Cuevas can use his hands and size to win occasional contested targets. He’ll need to claim more than a blocking role in Baltimore before you can expect a fantasy return.
Allen has generated useful gains on limited work, and his speed gives Kansas City a way to create space. He needs to expand beyond that role before he’s worth more than a deep stash.
Singleton is buried in Tennessee for now, but an unsettled veteran backfield gives the rookie a path to more work later. He's a stash for teams that can wait through a possible reset.
Thompson’s Mississippi State breakout showed what his speed can do when an offense gives him regular work. He’s a taxi-squad bet on the Chargers finding more ways to get him the ball.
Jones remains useful because he can contribute as both a runner and receiver. His age makes that a short-term edge, not a reason to count on another multi-year run as a starter.
Bech’s physical style fits an underneath role in Las Vegas, but he hasn’t earned enough regular work to give PPR managers a floor. He’s a deep stash if you can wait on the route share.
Hibner’s size can help in the red zone, and his blocking gives him a credible backup role. He needs to earn routes beyond those situations to have dynasty value.

The move to the Giants has given McCarthy a fresh chance to show what he can do, and his 2026 performances have offered some encouragement. He remains a speculative superflex hold until he shows he can sustain that progress.
Evans has shown some receiving promise in Carolina’s split tight end room. He’s an inexpensive stash for a bigger role, but not someone to rely on while that work stays spread out.
Bellinger’s contract gives him a plausible place in Tennessee’s rotation alongside Gunnar Helm. To matter in PPR, he’ll need a larger share of the passing work than his lineup status alone implies.
Robinson’s short targets give Tennessee an easy outlet and preserve some PPR value. He needs a lot of catches to make up for how rarely those throws turn into big gains.

McGowan has made enough of his opportunities for Indianapolis to keep developing him. Jonathan Taylor's extension makes the short-term value mostly insurance, with a larger role possible only if the backfield opens up.
Williams has made the most of his downfield chances with Drake Maye. That gives him a long-term ceiling, but he’ll need to win targets closer to the line of scrimmage to become a steady PPR option.
Mims is easier to hold in leagues that reward return yards. His special-teams value should keep him in the mix, but his modest receiving workload makes a PPR breakout hard to bank on.
Cousins can still offer usable passing production when a team needs a veteran starter. His dynasty value is in covering a contender's lineup, not in anchoring it across seasons.

Allgeier has shown in Arizona that he can carry the offense on the ground when needed, and he's under contract through 2027. Jeremiyah Love limits his path to a permanent lead role, but Allgeier has value as a power complement who can handle more.

McMillan has flashed when Tampa Bay gives him routes, but the team has added young receivers in the meantime. Hold him for a chance to win back a regular job, not because that opportunity is guaranteed.

Dobbins still has a role in Denver, but Jonah Coleman's emergence makes it hard to count on the veteran leading the backfield beyond 2026. His best long-term outcome may be as the experienced half of a committee.
Bentley can earn a backup role with his blocking and hands. He’s not a priority stash unless Denver gives him enough routes to show what he can do as a receiver.
Kacmarek’s blocking and reliable hands give him a path to Miami’s lineup. A blocking-heavy role won’t translate into fantasy value without more routes.
Tremble has a role in Carolina, but a shared workload limits his fantasy relevance. He needs either more regular routes or a clearer scoring-area role to be worth holding.
Royals has made some progress in Kansas City after a quiet rookie season. Josh Downs adds competition, so keep Royals on deep benches until he can earn routes without an opening ahead of him.
Coleman has flashed scoring upside out of the slot in Miami. The dynasty bet is on him turning those flashes into the kind of consistent underneath work that matters in PPR.
Bell’s college production and route detail make him worth developing, but Buffalo has more established receivers ahead of him. Keep him in deep leagues while he works toward regular routes.
Aiyuk remains an unsigned bet on talent rather than a source of lineup points. Wait for a landing spot and evidence of a regular workload before paying for his former ceiling.
Joly’s college receiving résumé gives him a reason to stand out in Miami’s young tight end room. He needs to turn that upside into regular NFL routes before he’s more than a deep stash.

Bigsby showed Philadelphia he can take on meaningful early-down work when Saquon Barkley is unavailable. That's enough to keep him in the dynasty picture, though his receiving limitations make a lasting lead role unlikely.
Musgrave has the athleticism to merit another look, but he hasn’t built a durable receiving role behind Tucker Kraft. He needs a clearer route to targets before a dynasty rebound makes sense.
Mumpfield has shown he can generate chunk plays in the Rams’ offense. Stash him in deeper builds if you can wait for a bigger role behind Puka Nacua and Davante Adams.
Watkins has turned limited opportunities into big gains for San Francisco. The speed is worth stashing, but he needs more than vertical routes to crack typical PPR lineups.
Jeudy hasn’t commanded consistent volume for Cleveland. With KC Concepcion and Denzel Boston in the mix, the former lead receiver needs to prove he can earn his targets rather than inherit them.
Sinnott is young enough to take a step, but Washington signing Chig Okonkwo makes the path narrower. Only hold him if your roster has room to wait for a clear increase in routes.
Endries can run routes from the slot or in line, giving Cincinnati some flexibility. With so many established targets ahead of him, he’s best left to deep developmental rosters.

Montgomery's move to Houston hasn't restored the workload or efficiency he showed at his best in Detroit. He can still offer power and short-yardage value, but his dynasty window is narrower than that of the younger backs in this tier.

Benson’s speed gives Las Vegas a reason to keep developing him as a deep threat. He needs to show he can earn catches on more than occasional shots before he’s worth a roster spot outside very deep leagues.
Tonges has shown he can fill in as a receiver when George Kittle is unavailable. Value the contingency, not an assumption that he’ll inherit Kittle’s role.
Knox can fill in when Dalton Kincaid is out and remains useful around the goal line. Value him as insurance, not as a bet on another run as Buffalo’s lead receiving tight end.

White's receiving profile gives him a better chance to stay relevant in PPR than his carry share alone suggests. Without a clear hold on Washington's lead job, he'll need those targets to remain a lineup option.
Mitchell's speed gives the Chargers a different look behind Omarion Hampton. His long-term value depends more on winning designed touches in space than on inheriting the whole backfield.
Sampson has a plausible PPR role as Cleveland's receiving complement to Quinshon Judkins. For him to graduate from a stash, the targets need to become a steady part of the offense.

Vidal has shown the Chargers he can handle a larger rushing role when called on. Omarion Hampton limits the path to a lead job, but Vidal's ability to take on more than a few carries gives him staying power in dynasty.

Randall's size and background at receiver give Baltimore several ways to develop him. Passing-down work would be his quickest route to a lasting role, and taking on more carries would lift his ceiling.

Tucker has shown he can make fill-in work count, but Tampa Bay has more established options for passing downs and lead carries. He needs a clearer lane in this backfield or a move to turn those flashes into lasting value.

Claiborne has breakaway speed, but injuries have limited what Minnesota has seen of him as a rookie. His chance to become more than a change-of-pace back depends on earning work as the veteran rotation turns over.
Hawes can earn snaps as a blocker and occasional red-zone option. Buffalo’s more established receiving tight ends leave him with a narrow path to relevant volume.
Nowakowski can add value as a blocker and underneath receiver. That flexibility can help him stick in Pittsburgh without giving him enough targets for fantasy.
Royer’s hands give him a shot at secondary receiving work, though blocking is the clearer route onto the field. Harold Fannin Jr. limits the fantasy opportunities available to a Cleveland backup.
Smith’s ability with the ball in his hands can still create a few useful designed touches. At his age and with Tucker Kraft ahead of him in Green Bay, there isn’t much reason to stash him.
Allen is part of a deep Rams rotation rather than a featured receiver. It would take a clearer share of routes for him to become more than emergency depth.
Briningstool’s receiving upside is worth tracking if Kansas City’s tight end room opens up. He first needs to earn a roster role before anyone should count on a succession path.
Dippre’s strength could earn him another look as a blocker. Without a team or an established receiving role, he’s a watchlist name rather than a stash.
Nailor has shown he can finish drives in the red zone. He’ll need more work between the 20s in Las Vegas to be more than a touchdown-dependent depth option.
Hill’s upside is still enticing, but he’s unsigned and has no role to project. Even contenders should price him as a speculative hold rather than a proven WR1.

Meyers has contributed enough in Cincinnati to hold in deep PPR. A regular role alongside Ja’Marr Chase and Tee Higgins would matter more for his dynasty stock than an occasional spike when one of them is out.
Lane’s speed gives Washington a reason to design touches for him. For dynasty, the signal to buy is when he starts earning work on ordinary dropbacks too.
Jennings showed he can handle starter volume in San Francisco, but that hasn’t carried over to a reliable role alongside Justin Jefferson. He’s depth in Minnesota until he earns a larger share.

Injuries and competition for snaps have clouded Murray's role in Minnesota. His rushing still gives him a path back to fantasy relevance, but he's no longer a player to value as a secure multi-year starter.
Robinson's downhill style makes him a natural complement to Bijan Robinson in Atlanta. Without steady receiving work, he'll need a different situation to become more than injury insurance in dynasty.
Johnson has begun to earn early-down work since arriving in Green Bay. A bigger piece of the rotation when Josh Jacobs is healthy would give him a much better chance to matter beyond this season.

Vaki has established a place behind Jahmyr Gibbs, giving Detroit a useful option when it needs more rushing depth. His dynasty upside is mostly as a potential fill-in unless the Lions entrust him with a regular share.

Lloyd's acceleration is worth betting on at a low price, but injuries have kept him from establishing a role in Green Bay. He has to move ahead of the other reserves before a future opening behind Josh Jacobs becomes meaningful.

Tracy's receiving background gives him a role even when Cam Skattebo handles the heavier carries. He can stay relevant across several seasons if the Giants keep him involved on passing downs, but his ceiling depends on winning a larger rushing share.
Davis gives Buffalo a sturdy early-down option behind James Cook. He has more value if he wins a clearer backup role or changes teams than if he remains in a small share of the Bills' backfield.
Wright hasn't seized a lead role even when Miami has needed alternatives to De’Von Achane. His speed makes him worth tracking, but Ollie Gordon II has the better claim to being Achane's understudy.
Ruckert’s blocking can keep him in the Jets’ rotation. Mason Taylor and Kenyon Sadiq make it hard to see where a meaningful target share would come from.
Stover needs to stay available and earn targets behind Dalton Schultz. Marlin Klein gives Houston another young option, so Stover can’t count on inheriting the job.
Sharp’s quarterback background leaves room for growth, but earning a reserve job behind Cade Otton comes first. He’s a watchlist option until Tampa Bay gives him receiving work.
Rogers has the athleticism to develop as a receiver, but Dallas already has a long-term starter in Jake Ferguson. His next milestone is earning offensive snaps.
Kanak produced in college despite being new to tight end, which keeps the developmental upside interesting. Tennessee’s competition and his learning curve make him a taxi-squad bet at most.
Schoonmaker offers reserve snaps behind Jake Ferguson. He needs more than a depth-chart opening to matter in fantasy; he also needs a regular role as a receiver.
Traore showed receiving promise in college, but Miami has several young tight ends competing for development time. He’s a name to monitor until there’s a clearer sign he can earn routes.
Gyllenborg showed downfield promise at Wyoming, but he’s a developmental option rather than an assumed successor in Kansas City. A steady role would be the first reason to move him up.

Allen’s arrival in San Francisco showed the veteran can still earn targets with his route running. He’s useful PPR depth for a contender, but rebuilding teams should put that roster spot toward a younger receiver.
Legette can still produce a big play outside, but he hasn’t settled into a consistent role opposite Tetairoa McMillan. His dynasty value depends on becoming more than a splash-play option.
Johnson has shown he can stretch a defense despite a limited role in Tampa Bay. That’s worth holding in deeper leagues, especially if he can earn routes without needing an opening ahead of him.
Young gives Cincinnati a bigger target who can stretch the field. Keep him on taxi squads while he works toward a regular outside role behind Chase and Higgins.
Williams brings size and playmaking to Green Bay’s designed-touch packages. To matter long term, he needs to earn regular routes behind Matthew Golden and Christian Watson.
Palmer has delivered big plays for Buffalo without much week-to-week volume. With D.J. Moore in the mix, he’s a depth piece until he claims steadier targets.
Whittington’s path to PPR relevance depends on more playing time behind the Rams’ established receivers. Hold him only where you can afford to wait for that opening.
Daniels carved out meaningful work in Miami’s college passing game. He’s a taxi-squad candidate with the Rams until he can find a regular spot in the rotation.
Burks has the quickness to work inside, but late draft capital and a small role in Indianapolis leave little room for a slow climb. Keep him on watch lists rather than using an active roster spot.

Watson has shown occasional passing upside in 2026, but Cleveland has also given Shedeur Sanders a look. Value Watson for the starts he can earn rather than assuming the job is his beyond this season.
Knight has shown he can make the most of fill-in work in Arizona, but he's on a one-year deal. His dynasty case depends on earning a similar or better opening after this season.

Kamara still adds value as a receiver, but the Saints no longer need him to handle the entire backfield. With his deal running through 2026, he's a shorter-window dynasty asset whose next role matters more than his past production.

Brooks' college workload gives him the profile to take on more carries if Cincinnati's backfield changes. To gain lasting dynasty value, he needs to show he can earn regular work rather than merely fill in behind Chase Brown.

Kiner has made productive use of his opportunities in New England this season. He's worth tracking as the rotation evolves, but he still needs to show he can keep a meaningful workload when the backfield is healthy.

Hill's receiving and pass protection make him useful alongside a power runner, a role he can carry forward even if Baltimore's backfield changes. The lack of a clear path to lead carries keeps his dynasty ceiling modest.
James has the vision and burst to fit San Francisco's rushing scheme. He needs to get past the backs in front of him before that fit can turn into a multi-year fantasy role.

Shipley's hands offer a path to change-of-pace work in Philadelphia, but injuries have made it hard to establish a role. He's a developmental hold whose value rises if he can win regular passing downs.
Trigg can create yards after the catch, which gives him upside if a team gives him a chance. First he needs to stick on a roster and show he can earn routes.
Reiman can complement Trey McBride as a blocker, but that doesn't put him in line for McBride's targets. He needs a role change before he’s worth stashing outside the deepest leagues.
Maryland showed receiving ability at SMU and has time to develop. Wait for a roster spot and a plausible path to routes before using a dynasty spot on him.
Culp’s athleticism makes him worth tracking if he lands in a receiving-friendly situation. There’s not enough established production to roster him without one.
Hutchinson has made a useful contribution in Houston despite competition from younger receivers. He’s worth holding for depth in deeper formats, but the competition limits his multi-year ceiling.
Lambert-Smith has taken a step forward from a quiet rookie season, but he’s still competing for regular outside snaps. He’s a developmental hold for deep Chargers stashes.
Thornton’s size and speed give him plenty of upside on the perimeter. Buy only if the Raiders start using him as a regular target instead of counting on the traits alone.
Mooney has shown he can produce when he gets volume, but the Giants haven’t leaned on him that way. Treat him as roster depth behind Malik Nabers rather than paying for a return to his Atlanta peak.
Ridley’s production has fallen off, and Tennessee has added Carnell Tate. Hold only as inexpensive veteran depth unless Ridley earns a bigger share again.
Kupp can still help a deep contender, but Jaxon Smith-Njigba owns the high-volume role in Seattle. His value is in short-term coverage rather than a rebuilding roster spot.

Johnson can handle physical carries in a pinch, but Chicago has shown more commitment to D'Andre Swift and Kyle Monangai. A change in the rotation or a new team may be his best chance to regain dynasty value.

Conner's physical running can still help when he's healthy, but injury and Arizona's investment in Jeremiyah Love have narrowed his dynasty window. He's a speculative hold rather than a dependable contender option.
Pacheco's injury has left Sione Vaki to handle backup work behind Jahmyr Gibbs. For Pacheco to regain lasting value, he needs to show he can stay on the field and win a place in a rotation again.
Burks has made some plays downfield in Washington. He merits a deep bench spot for that upside, but needs steadier targets before PPR managers can trust his floor.
Iosivas has shown he can step in when Cincinnati needs a receiver. With Chase and Higgins available, he’s more useful as insurance than as a player to build around.
Dotson has made good use of downfield chances in Atlanta. The modest catch volume limits his usefulness in PPR, but the big-play role fits deep best-ball builds.
Virgil’s catch radius and speed give Arizona another way to attack downfield. He’s a taxi-squad stash if you have room to see whether he can grow into more than a vertical specialist.
Thornton can stretch the field for Kansas City without getting fed targets. That makes him easier to roster in best ball, where you don’t have to pick the right week for a deep ball to hit.

Richardson's rushing upside is worth holding in deep superflex, even without a clear path to snaps in Indianapolis. He needs another opportunity to prove he can turn that athleticism into a starting job that lasts.

Singletary is an experienced fill-in, but his 2026 work hasn't pointed to an expanding role. Cam Skattebo and Tyrone Tracy Jr. give the Giants younger options, limiting Singletary's appeal beyond this season.
Davis has the patience and power to handle more early-down work if the Jets' backfield changes. Breece Hall and Braelon Allen leave Davis needing a clear opportunity to climb beyond depth value.

Etienne has the hands to carve out a passing-down role, but Chuba Hubbard commands the workload that matters most in Carolina. A defined receiving job would give Etienne a reason to hold even without a path to lead carries.

Wilson has shown he can take on carries when needed, but Seattle's investment in Jadarian Price points to a younger option for the long term. Wilson has more value as dependable depth than as a bet on a future lead role.

Heidenreich's receiving background gives Pittsburgh more than one way to use him. His dynasty value depends on whether that versatility earns a defined offensive role rather than an occasional package.

Sanders brings appealing burst for a bigger back, but he hasn't built a clear path to regular work in Cleveland. He's a developmental lottery ticket whose value depends on turning those traits into an NFL role.

Estime has earned a place in New Orleans' early-down rotation despite a crowded backfield. He needs a larger share of the rushing work to sustain fantasy value because catches aren't his main route to production.

New Orleans moved on from Hunter, so his next opportunity will matter more than his old depth-chart spot. His contact balance leaves some developmental appeal if another team gives him a chance at early-down work.
Allen's vision and tempo give him a case for early-down work in Miami. His modest draft investment makes him a long shot for sustained volume unless he can separate from the other depth backs.
Ali offers quickness behind Baltimore's power backs, but he hasn't established a dependable role. He needs to separate from the other reserves to become meaningful dynasty insurance.
Miller has landed on Dallas' practice squad rather than in a backfield rotation. Until he earns an active-roster opportunity and shows he can handle steady work, he's strictly a deep dynasty hold.
Smith’s speed can threaten defenses vertically, but he hasn’t found a dependable receiving role. Keep him on the watch list with Omar Cooper Jr. competing for routes.
Felton has contributed in spots, but special teams remains his clearest path to game-day work. He’ll need to carve out a receiving role in Minnesota to make a dynasty roster.
Arizona's willingness to give Beck a look is more significant for dynasty than his early results. He needs to show enough as a passer to turn that opportunity into a lasting role.
Smith has taken care of the ball well for the Jets in 2026, which keeps him useful when he plays. Think of him as a superflex bridge rather than a quarterback to build around.

Jones has had starting opportunities in Indianapolis without turning 2026 into a strong case for a long-term job. He's a superflex option if you can use the starts, not a quarterback to count on across seasons.

Smith's receiver background gives Kansas City a way to get him touches in space. With Kenneth Walker and Emmett Johnson better positioned for carries, Smith needs a durable receiving role to deliver fantasy value.

Allen's receiving ability gives him a path to PPR value that doesn't require winning Jacksonville's lead rushing job. Bhayshul Tuten limits that rushing upside, making a steady passing-down role the key to Allen's outlook.
Wetjen’s return ability gives him his clearest route to playing time. He’s worth knowing in return-yardage leagues, while standard PPR managers should wait for an offensive role.
Walker has shown he can make something out of a downfield target. Baltimore needs to send more of those chances his way before he’s useful in PPR.
Turpin can turn returns and designed touches into big gains. That gives him a clearer fantasy fit in return-scoring leagues than in conventional PPR.
Cowing has flashed enough to keep watching, but the 49ers’ veteran additions limit his path to snaps. He’s a deep stash until he wins a role of his own.

Giddens has the size and quickness to develop into a useful reserve runner. With Jonathan Taylor established, the long-term bet is on Giddens becoming the clear next man up rather than on immediate volume.
Goodson showed he can step in for Dallas, but injury interrupted his bid to hold the backup job. He needs to reclaim a consistent role for that fill-in production to carry dynasty value.
Atwell can still stretch a defense for the Rams. That speed plays better as occasional best-ball upside than as a source of regular PPR points.
Raymond has done enough to help as short-term depth in deep PPR leagues. Chicago’s investment in Luther Burden III and Rome Odunze makes Raymond a poor fit for a rebuild.

Brissett has shown in Baltimore that he can handle a substantial passing workload when called on. That gives him value as superflex insurance, but Lamar Jackson's presence limits the appeal of betting on a lasting starting role.
Johnson can catch passes and protect the QB behind James Cook, but his Buffalo deal runs through 2026. His dynasty outlook depends on finding a team willing to give him a steady receiving role.

Perine's receiving and pass protection keep him useful in Cincinnati, but the Bengals haven't needed him to carry the backfield. His value is mostly short-term insurance, with little reason to project a larger role over time.
Williams was a productive possession receiver at Stanford. The Jacksonville depth chart gives him time to develop, but it’s also why he belongs on a watch list rather than most benches.
Sturdivant has shown enough as an undrafted receiver to get on deep watch lists. Look for Green Bay to give him consistent routes before spending a roster spot.
McCaffrey has flashed when Washington has needed help at receiver. He’s a deep watch-list option until the team gives him consistent routes without relying on absences ahead of him.
Bond was a steady target at Boston College and can create after the catch. Until he finds an NFL roster, give your stash spots to receivers already earning snaps.
Robinson gives San Francisco a veteran it can turn to when it needs depth. He can fill a short-term bench need in the deepest leagues but offers little reason to carry him through a rebuild.
Cleveland has given Sanders a chance to show what he can do in 2026, but hasn't established him as its long-term answer. He belongs on deep superflex benches while the team evaluates him.

Guerendo's speed remains intriguing, but injuries and the emergence of Kaelon Black have kept him from establishing a place behind Christian McCaffrey. His dynasty case depends on staying healthy and earning back a real share of the rotation.
Herbert hasn't carved out a meaningful rushing role in Atlanta behind Bijan Robinson. He's emergency depth in deep leagues unless a new opportunity gives him more than sporadic carries.

Trayanum has the size to compete for short-yardage work, but the Jets have younger backs with stronger claims on carries. He needs to find a reliable roster role before those traits make him worth stashing.

Demercado has shown useful efficiency in relief and can contribute on passing downs. With Woody Marks and David Montgomery in Houston, Demercado needs a lasting specialty role rather than an opening to lead the backfield.
Metchie has been useful in spots for Carolina. He’s a deep PPR hold if he can turn those opportunities into regular work behind Tetairoa McMillan.
Law has the versatility to play inside or outside. Keep him on a deep taxi squad if you can wait to see where Detroit gives him a path to targets.
Caldwell’s size and athleticism are intriguing, but an undrafted prospect needs a chance to turn them into routes. Keep him on the watch list unless he carves out a role in Kansas City.
Horn’s speed gives him a way to get on the field through special teams. With Cleveland adding young receivers, wait for actual offensive work before committing a dynasty spot.
Milroe's rushing makes him a compelling stash if he develops into a starting-caliber passer. Sam Darnold leaves him without a clear path to snaps, so treat him as a multi-year project.
Blue's speed has helped him earn return work in Philadelphia, but that doesn't guarantee offensive touches. He's a taxi-squad option until his quickness earns him a role on passing downs or in space.

Donaldson's power gives him a shot to stick as a short-yardage back, but his receiving profile limits the long-term ceiling. He needs to turn that specialized skill into a reliable role to matter in deep leagues.

Ott flashed lead-back and receiving ability early in college, but injuries and a quiet finish make that upside speculative. His dynasty value depends on turning those flashes into a defined role in Kansas City.
Davis is most interesting when your league scores return yards. The Chargers can use his speed on occasional touches, but that isn’t enough for a conventional PPR hold.

Tagovailoa needs a steady starting job to have much dynasty appeal because he adds little on the ground. Atlanta has given Michael Penix Jr. the lead role, leaving Tua as a bet on an opportunity rather than established production.

Daniels showed enough mobility in relief to be worth tracking in deep superflex. He needs more time to develop as a passer before there's a reason to project a future beyond backing up Baker Mayfield.
Gould can contribute as a returner and flash as a receiver in Indianapolis. Only return-scoring leagues give him a strong reason to be rostered without steadier targets.
McCulley showed he can win outside as a bigger receiver at Michigan. He went undrafted, so put him on the watch list in Miami rather than using a roster spot before he earns a role.
Rodgers can still provide serviceable passing production for a contender. His dynasty value is tied to the starts you can use, not to a role you can count on across seasons.
Mariota's legs can make him a useful emergency start behind Jayden Daniels. There's little long-term upside unless he finds a clearer path to playing time.

Leonard has a difficult path to playing time behind Daniel Jones and Anthony Richardson. He's worth tracking only in the deepest superflex leagues unless Indianapolis gives him a real opportunity to develop on the field.
